title: Variance versus TypeScript
hook: IEnumerable<string> is an IEnumerable<object> because T only comes out. IList<string> is not an IList<object> because you could put a Dog in. TypeScript’s structural typing and function bivariance will lie to you if you import them into C#.

sections.heading: out and in
sections.prose: Covariance (out T): a producer of T can be used as a producer of a base type. IEnumerable<out T>, IReadOnlyList<out T>, Func<out TResult>. IEnumerable<string> → IEnumerable<object> is legal. Contravariance (in T): a consumer of T can be used as a consumer of a derived type. Action<in T>, IComparer<in T>. Action<object> can be assigned to Action<string> because anything that handles object can handle string. Type parameters on classes and structs are invariant — only interfaces and delegates declare variance, and only for reference types. You cannot write IEnumerable<out int> conversions from IEnumerable<int> to IEnumerable<object> because int is a value type.

snippets.label: Covariance and contravariance
snippets.explanation: Read-only sequences can widen the element type. Mutating lists cannot. Callbacks can narrow the input type.

sections.heading: Why arrays still surprise people
sections.prose: string[] to object[] is allowed (array covariance) and can throw ArrayTypeMismatchException on write. Generics fixed that for List<T>. If an interviewer says “are C# generics covariant?,” the precise answer is: constructed generic classes are invariant; annotated interfaces and delegates can be variant; arrays are the historical hole.

sections.heading: TypeScript comparison
sections.prose: TypeScript infers variance structurally. ReadonlyArray<string> is a ReadonlyArray<string | number> in some positions because TS treats readonly arrays covariantly. Function parameters are bivariant under default compiler flags unless strictFunctionTypes is on — then they are contravariant, closer to C#. There is no out keyword on TS interfaces; compatibility is structural. Do not say “TS is covariant like IEnumerable.” Say “TS structural typing plus (historically) bivariant callbacks; C# variance is opt-in on interfaces and checked.”

interviewTakeaways: out T = covariant producer; in T = contravariant consumer; classes are invariant.
Value types do not participate in variant conversions.
TS function bivariance is not the C# rule; enable strictFunctionTypes for a fair comparison.
commonPitfalls: Declaring a variant interface that uses T in both input and output positions (illegal).
Citing array covariance as proof that List is covariant.

jsTsCorrelations.note: strictFunctionTypes makes callback parameters contravariant, aligning with Action<in T>. ReadonlyArray is covariant like IEnumerable<out T>.
